title: NPT bound entanglement
formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.
why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

progress.text: The Horodeckis prove the partial-transpose obstruction and establish bound entanglement in the PPT regime.
DiVincenzo and coauthors develop structured NPT candidates and evidence for undistillability.
Fu–Gao–Park submit a proof of the exact two-copy threshold for all Werner dimensions; v2 follows on 27 July.
Fraser–Huber–Pozsgay–Vona derive the threshold from a general rank-constrained partial-trace inequality.
Bharti–Gajjala–Haug give another two-copy proof and restricted finite-copy extensions, explicitly retaining the all-copy question.
Wu–Zou prove three-copy endpoint inequalities for specified coefficient-operator sectors; the general problem remains unresolved.

On 16 September 2026 the original primary papers, full cached July 2026 two-copy statements and three-copy introduction, current arXiv revision records and a bounded later-work search were checked. The two-copy thresholds and restricted three-copy sectors do not prove or refute the all-copy target. context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The open problem therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal investigated NPT states whose one-copy behavior differs from their spectral negativity. Their evidence did not establish one fixed NPT state undistillable for every finite number of copies. The present question retains that full order of quantifiers.

The Werner family is \(\rho_{\mathrm W}(d,\alpha)=(I+\alpha F)/(d^2+\alpha d)\), for \(d\ge2\) and \(-1\le\alpha\le1\), where \(F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u\) swaps the two local systems and \(I\) is identity. Its members are NPT exactly for \(\alpha<-1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly for \(\alpha<-1/2\). Thus \(-1/2\le\alpha<-1/d\) is the NPT one-copy-undistillable interval when \(d\ge3\). This is a known subclass; the target is not restricted to Werner states.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

Bharti, Gajjala and Haug also obtain the two-copy threshold and several restricted finite-copy extensions, while explicitly leaving the general all-copy assertion open. A family of states indexed by the allowed number of copies does not give the single fixed state required by the existential target.

Wu and Zou prove three-copy endpoint nonnegativity for specified sectors, including normal rank-two coefficient operators. A coefficient operator is the matrix of a bipartite test vector in product bases; normal means that the matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. Other rank-two matrices are allowed in the full criterion, so these sector results do not settle unrestricted three-copy distillability or the all-copy question.

sentences: Entangled states can sometimes be converted into nearly perfect shared Bell pairs using many copies and local operations with classical communication.
Bound entanglement means that this distillation remains impossible despite the presence of entanglement.
The question asks whether such states can have a negative partial transpose, a spectral property associated with distillability in simpler settings.
Failure of a protocol on one copy or any fixed number of copies does not establish the required obstruction for every number of copies.
Resolving the question would sharpen the distinction between entanglement as a property and entanglement as a usable communication resource.
